notes.meaning: David begs God not to correct him in anger. He is not asking to escape correction. He asks God to correct him gently, as a loving Father, not as an angry judge. The title 'for remembrance' means the psalm helps David and others remember how God corrects His people for sin.

God's 'arrows' and heavy 'hand' are word-pictures. They show how deeply David feels God's displeasure, in his body and even more in his conscience. Such arrows stick fast until God Himself pulls them out and heals the wound.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the arrows as God's words. Once fixed in the heart, they stir up love and a longing for the rest God promises.

notes.meaning: David's body has no health and his bones have no rest. God's anger is the near cause, but David names the deeper cause: his own sin. He does not blame God. He admits he brought this on himself. The old Prayer Book confession, 'there is no health in us,' draws on words like these.
David's sins feel like floodwaters over his head, or a load too heavy to carry. Spurgeon says it is good when sin feels this heavy. Though it is too heavy for us, Jesus carried it.

His wounds smell and fester. Some writers take this as a real disease, and others as a picture of a sick soul. 'Folly' here means sin, which is the most foolish thing of all. Henry says sins, like wounds, get worse when we leave them alone and do not confess them. Teachers add that the verse does not mean every illness comes from a person's own sin.
David is bent over and goes about mourning all day. Pain bends the body, and guilt bends the soul down in shame. Nothing brings a person lower than a sense of sin and of God's displeasure.
His lower body burns with pain, and nothing in him is healthy. The word suggests a burning, feverish illness. Wesley says we should take the words as a real disease unless we have good reason not to.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The NET Bible notes that the Hebrew can read 'my loins are filled with shame.' On that reading, the loins stand for the place of deep feeling.

notes.meaning: David feels numb and crushed, and he groans aloud from the pain in his heart. The Geneva notes say his example teaches us never to despair. However great the pain, we should keep crying to God for help. Henry sees David here as a picture of Christ in His agony.

In the middle of his pain, David takes comfort that God sees everything. God knows all he longs for and hears every groan, even ones he cannot put into words. This links with Romans 8:26, where the Spirit prays for us with groans too deep for words.

His heart races, his strength is gone, and his eyes grow dim. This may come from weeping, weakness, or fainting. David the brave warrior is now as weak as water. Sickness can humble even the strongest person.

Friends and even family keep their distance from his illness. Clarke thinks they saw him as under God's judgment and feared catching his disease. Hard times show who true friends are. We have a Friend in heaven who never stands far off. Henry and Spurgeon compare this to those who watched Jesus' cross from a distance.
While friends pull away, enemies move in. They set traps, speak of his ruin, and plot all day. They hide their harmful plans behind a friendly face.

David acts as if he cannot hear their attacks, and he gives no answer. Henry says he kept calm and left his defence to God. Others say his own guilt left him with nothing to say, or that his silence showed he humbly accepted his correction. Both Henry and Spurgeon see here a picture of Jesus, who stayed silent before His accusers.
This is why David can stay quiet: he is waiting for God. He is sure God will answer and stand up for him. Nothing has changed yet, but by faith he says, 'You will answer.'
David asks God not to let his enemies gloat when he stumbles. If God does not help, they will mock him as if God had left him. So the prayer is also about God's honour.

David feels close to falling, and his pain never leaves him. Henry says he was near to grumbling against God and losing his temper with his attackers. Keeping our eyes on our sorrow makes us stumble. Keeping our eyes on God keeps us standing.

David openly confesses his sin to God and is truly sorry for it. Henry says real repentance (turning from sin back to God) has two parts. One is honest confession, and the other is heartfelt sorrow. Spurgeon adds that sorrow does not pay for sin, but it is the right spirit in which to come to Jesus, who saves.

His enemies are many and strong, and they hate him for no good reason. Older English Bibles say the enemies are 'lively.' Clarke and Keil & Delitzsch explain that a very small change in one Hebrew letter gives 'without cause,' as here. Spurgeon notes that however weak a believer is, the forces against us never get tired. So we must keep praying.

These enemies pay back his kindness with evil and attack him for doing what is right. This does not cancel his confession. A person can be guilty before God and still innocent of wronging other people. David would rather be hated by everyone than fail in his duty to God.

David ends with urgent prayer. Others have left him, so he asks God not to leave him too, and to come quickly. The psalm ends without relief, but he still calls God 'my Savior.' True repentance gives up hope in itself but never gives up hope in God.
